title: Choosing Linear, Quadratic and Exponential Models
seo_title: Algebra II Data and Regression Models Worksheets (TEKS 2A.8A–2A.8C)
standard_text: 2A.8A analyze data to select the appropriate model from among linear, quadratic, and exponential models; 2A.8B use regression methods available through technology to write a linear function, a quadratic function, and an exponential function from a given set of data; 2A.8C predict and make decisions and critical judgments from a given set of data using linear, quadratic, and exponential models
meta_desc: Free Algebra II data worksheets for Texas TEKS 2A.8A to 2A.8C: choose linear, quadratic or exponential models, predict with regression, interpret models and judge fits. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Same differences: linear. Same second differences: quadratic. Same ratios: exponential.
key_sub: r² close to 1 means a good fit.
body_html:
How to think about it

  • Linear: the first differences are the same (a constant amount each step).
  • Quadratic: the second differences are the same.
  • Exponential: the ratios are the same (a constant factor or percent each step).
  • A calculator's regression gives the equation; r2 close to 1 means a good fit.
  • Predictions inside the data range are safer than predictions far outside it.

Examples

Example

y: 3, 6, 12, 24, 48

Ratios: 2, 2, 2, 2

Answer: Exponential: y = 3(2)x

Example

y = 1,200(1.04)x

1.04 = 1 + 0.04

Answer: 4% growth each year

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Looking only at first differencesCheck second differences and ratios too.
Reading 1.06 as 106% growth1.06 means 6% growth.
Trusting a prediction far outside the dataExtrapolation may not hold.
